strengths: Introduces the first anytime NAS benchmark and framework tailored to tabular data, including a new benchmark dataset (NAS-Bench-Tabular) with 160,000 architectures fully trained across three real-world datasets, which is a valuable resource for the community.

Conducts a thorough empirical study of nine existing zero-cost proxies on tabular data, an area that was previously unexplored, and provides useful negative/positive findings (e.g., NTK-based proxies transfer poorly to tabular DNNs).

Proposes ExpressFlow, a new zero-cost proxy grounded in a theoretical connection to synaptic saliency and neuron-wise aggregation, with reasonably rigorous derivations relating it to trainability and expressivity, and demonstrates consistently higher SRCC than prior proxies across three datasets and even reasonable transfer to image NAS benchmarks.

The two-phase filtering-refinement design with a budget-aware coordinator is a sensible and practical way to combine cheap training-free evaluation with more reliable training-based evaluation under a strict time budget, and the formalized objective (Eq. 2) gives an interpretable way to allocate budget.

Extensive appendices provide ablations (initialization, batch size, recalibration weights, data-agnostic property), sensitivity analysis of M/K and U, noise-robustness checks, and additional baselines (warmup/move-proposal combinations, one-shot/weight-sharing NAS), which substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Reports large empirical speedups over RE-NAS/TabNAS while matching or exceeding global-best AUC, and the anytime property (completing search within seconds while improving with more budget) is demonstrated across three datasets.
weaknesses: The search space is a very simple 4-layer fully-connected MLP with only per-layer width choices; it does not include richer architectural elements common in tabular DNN literature (e.g., attention, embeddings, feature interactions, residual connections), which limits how representative the benchmark and search results are of realistic tabular architecture design choices.

The headline claim of 'up to 82.75x' speedup is not representative of all settings — the Diabetes dataset only shows a 1.75x speedup, and the abstract/framing emphasizes the best case rather than giving a balanced picture of variability across datasets.

Baseline comparisons for the full ATLAS pipeline are limited to RE-NAS and TabNAS; other modern tabular NAS or hyperparameter optimization approaches (e.g., BOHB-based full pipelines, more recent transformer/attention-based tabular NAS) are not included as end-to-end anytime baselines, making the significance claim relative to the broader field harder to assess.

The coordinator's key ratios (M/K≈30, U=2) are tuned empirically per benchmark and it is unclear how sensitive/generalizable these settings are to different search space sizes, dataset scales, or hardware, raising reproducibility/generalization concerns beyond the three studied datasets.

Only three tabular datasets (Frappe, Diabetes, Criteo) are used for the main NAS-Bench-Tabular and ATLAS evaluation, which is a relatively narrow empirical base for a method claiming general applicability to 'tabular data' broadly.

Some theoretical contribution (ExpressFlow) is an incremental extension/re-derivation of existing synaptic-saliency-based proxies (e.g., SynFlow) via neuron-wise aggregation and recalibration, and while the derivation is clean, the conceptual novelty relative to prior trainability/expressivity proxies is moderate.

Error bars/variance reporting in the main text figures (e.g., Figure 6) are shown as shaded regions but the number of repeated runs and variance sources (search stochasticity, architecture initialization) are not always clearly specified within the main paper.

strengths: The paper tackles an underexplored niche (anytime NAS for tabular DNNs) and provides a reasonably complete artifact: a 160K-architecture benchmark (NAS-Bench-Tabular), a new zero-cost proxy (ExpressFlow), and a two-phase filtering/refinement search procedure, accompanied by code and detailed appendices.

The theoretical derivation connecting ExpressFlow to synaptic saliency/SynFlow (Appendix G.3) is a useful sanity check that grounds the proxy in existing theory rather than presenting it as purely heuristic.

Extensive ablations are provided (initialization method, batch size, parameter positivity, recalibration weights, noise injection, M/K and U sensitivity), which is good experimental hygiene and aids reproducibility.
The NAS research best-practices checklist and the reported hyperparameter search for the benchmark construction show attention to reproducibility concerns common in the NAS literature.
weaknesses: The search space is extremely narrow: a fixed 4-layer MLP where only the per-layer width is searched from a small discrete set. This is closer to hyperparameter tuning than architecture search, and it undermines the generality of claims about "Neural Architecture Search on Tabular Data" as a broad contribution.

Evaluation is limited to only three datasets (Frappe, Diabetes, Criteo-subset), all binary classification tasks of modest scale; no comparison against strong, standard tabular baselines (e.g., gradient-boosted trees, FT-Transformer, SAINT) is provided, so it is unclear whether the NAS-discovered MLPs are even competitive with well-known tabular methods, which is a central concern for any tabular-data paper.

The reported speedup (82.75x) is highly dataset-dependent and not representative: on Diabetes the speedup drops to only 1.75x, and the AUC improvements across datasets are often within a fraction of a percentage point (e.g., Frappe AUC gains of ~0.3 pp), raising questions about the practical significance of the claimed gains.

The budget-aware coordinator's core hyperparameters (M/K≈30, U=2) are determined empirically on the same benchmark/datasets used for evaluation, with no demonstration that these ratios transfer to new search spaces, architectures beyond 4-layer MLPs, or larger/more diverse tabular datasets — raising concerns about overfitting the coordinator design to the specific benchmark.

The novelty of the two-phase scheme is incremental relative to existing zero-cost-proxy-plus-training-based combinations (e.g., the "warmup" and "move-proposal" strategies from Abdelfattah et al. 2021 that the paper itself compares against); the main distinguishing element is the successive-halving scheduling plus a time-budget allocation heuristic, which is a relatively modest methodological advance.

The search space itself differs across datasets (e.g., Criteo uses a different, smaller H than Frappe/Diabetes), which complicates claims of a unified, comprehensive benchmark and could affect fairness of cross-dataset comparisons.

Variance/robustness reporting is limited to shaded bands in figures without reported statistical tests, and all "training" evaluation is done by querying a precomputed table rather than live training, so some of the reported run-to-run variability reflects search-strategy randomness rather than true architecture training noise — this should be made explicit as a limitation.

The explicit "Limitations" and "societal impact" discussions are essentially absent or marked N/A in the checklist, despite the method's reliance on empirically tuned constants and a narrow benchmark; a more candid discussion of when ExpressFlow/ATLAS might fail (e.g., different depths, categorical-heavy datasets, imbalanced tasks) is missing.

strengths: Novel problem framing: the paper formalizes 'anytime NAS' for tabular data, a practically relevant setting (e.g., bounded cloud budgets) that has not been previously studied.

Construction of NAS-Bench-Tabular, a benchmark of 160,000 fully trained architectures across three real datasets (Frappe, Diabetes, Criteo), which could be a useful community resource for future NAS-on-tabular research, reducing the cost of future evaluation.

Systematic benchmarking of nine existing zero-cost proxies on tabular data (not previously studied in this setting), providing useful empirical insight (e.g., that several vision-oriented proxies transfer poorly to tabular DNNs).

The proposed proxy ExpressFlow is given a careful theoretical derivation (Appendix G.3) connecting it to synaptic saliency/SynFlow at a neuron-wise level, offering some principled justification beyond pure empiricism.
Extensive ablation studies on initialization, batch size, recalibration weighting, noise robustness, and the M/K, U sensitivity analysis for the coordinator, which support the design choices.

Reported wall-clock speedups (up to 82.75x) over RE-NAS/TabNAS are substantial and the anytime behavior (completing within very small budgets, improving with larger budgets) is empirically demonstrated across all three datasets.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: code/data link provided, detailed hyperparameter tables, and a completed NAS best-practices checklist.
weaknesses: The search space is quite restrictive: a fixed 4-layer MLP backbone where only per-layer widths are searched, excluding other architectural choices (embeddings, feature interactions, attention, skip connections) common in tabular DNN literature, which limits how representative 'NAS-Bench-Tabular' is as a general benchmark and how broadly ATLAS's claims generalize.

Only three tabular datasets are used, and performance on Diabetes is comparatively unstable/noisy (large validation AUC spread in Fig. 2b, flatter anytime curves in Fig. 6b), raising concerns about the robustness and generality of the reported gains across more diverse real-world tabular tasks.

The budget-aware coordinator's key hyperparameters (M/K≈30, U=2) are determined empirically via grid-style sensitivity sweeps on the same benchmark datasets rather than derived from a principled theoretical argument; it is unclear how well these fixed ratios transfer to datasets/search spaces outside the three studied, creating a risk of overfitting the coordinator design to the benchmark.

There is potential circularity/self-referential evaluation: the zero-cost proxy, the search algorithm, and the benchmark used to validate them are all constructed by the same authors on the same three datasets, with no fully independent/external benchmark (outside the small image-domain transferability check) used to validate ExpressFlow or ATLAS end-to-end.

Baselines for the main anytime comparison (RE-NAS, TabNAS) both operate under training-based evaluation only and were not specifically designed for anytime behavior, so the comparison may be somewhat favorable to ATLAS by construction; stronger or more diverse anytime/multi-fidelity baselines (e.g., other BO+Hyperband variants, learning-curve extrapolation methods) are not deeply explored in the main text (only lightly touched in the appendix).

The theoretical novelty of ExpressFlow is incremental—it is shown to be mathematically equivalent to an aggregated/recalibrated form of existing synaptic saliency (SynFlow)-style scores, so the core technical contribution is more of a careful re-engineering/combination than a fundamentally new idea.

Limitations and societal impact discussions in the checklist are marked largely as 'Yes'/'N/A' without substantive discussion in the main text, leaving open questions about failure cases (e.g., why Diabetes anytime curves are flatter) unaddressed.
